div.head: Preface
div.p: This edition of King Lear, though intended to supersede that published by Horace Howard Furness in 1880, is not merely a revision or updating of it. The work of collating the texts and compiling the commentary and appendix has been done over again from the primary sources, Dr. Furness’s being treated as one of the long series of editions of the play. Dr. Furness’s edition, however, is not hereby rendered useless: on many points the opinions of early commentators are more fully represented there than here. With a few exceptions the survey of scholarly and editorial publication ends at the millennial year 2000.

This edition differs somewhat from earlier volumes of the New Variorum Shakespeare, following the guidelines for the series described in the Shakespeare Variorum Handbook (1971; rev. 2003) and approved by the New Variorum Shakespeare Committee of the Modern Language Association. The text is based primarily on the first printed edition of the play, the First Quarto of 1608, and includes some 110 additional lines from the First Folio of 1623. The choice of the Quarto as the primary text, and the editorial treatment of it and of the Folio additions, are discussed in the Plan of the Work. As in the most recent volumes in the New Variorum series, textual collations are recorded in condensed formulas using sigla for editions and for some manuscript commentaries; these sigla are identified in the Plan of the Work and (for ease of reference in the printed edition) in this volume’s end-paper paste-ins. Conjectural emendations of the text that were never adopted by any editor are not included in the textual notes but are relegated to an appendix. In order to make the edition as useful as possible for theatrical as well as scholarly purposes, the stage history of the play is described in two appendices, one recounting significant performances of the play, the other surveying changes to the text of the play on the stage as these have been recorded in adaptations, printed acting editions, and promptbooks.

Editorial work was divided and carried on concurrently by three different editors. The two-part survey of the stage history from 1681 onwards was written by Dr. Paula Glatzer; the survey of interpretive criticism was written by Dr. Kevin Donovan, who also contributed much material towards the commentary notes and prepared an early version of the text; Richard Knowles did the rest.

The editors are pleased to acknowledge the many forms of assistance which made this volume possible. More than to anyone else the Variorum series as a whole owes its present existence and impetus to the unflagging support of its former General Editor, Robert K. Turner, whose labors, expertise, and example have profited, guided, and inspired a whole generation of editors, Variorum and otherwise. With untiring attention and astringent skepticism the present General Editor, Paul Werstine, has uncovered countless errors, tightened arguments, added new insights, and changed every part of this edition for the better. Moreover, without his generous care, intelligence, and persistence in identifying and locating the targets of the countless, often fugitive cross-references made throughout its various parts, this edition in its present form would not have been completed. The same can be said of the accurate and immensely helpful index prepared by Dr. Denise Lamb. My thanks to the new General Editor, Eric Rasmussen, for his deep appreciation of this edition and his care seeing it through the press. Members of the Variorum Committee, especially David Bevington, Jay Halio, A. R. Braunmuller, and William Carroll, read parts of the manuscript and suggested improvements, as did Leeds Barroll, Michael Warren, Lois Potter, and Peter Blayney. I would like to give particular thanks to the member of the Committee who offered constant encouragement about the value of the Variorum project, the distinguished editor Barbara Mowat. A special debt is owed to the many revisionist textual scholars of the last quarter-century, whose vigorous challenges to accepted ideas about the texts of the play have stimulated radical rethinking and new insights; their arguments and responses to them occupy much of the commentary. The contributions of the many past giants of scholarship on the play—Horace H. Furness, Walter Greg, Madeleine Doran, and Kenneth Muir, among others—will be evident throughout the volume. Less evident, and too often taken for granted, is the work of the many bibliographers of Shakespeare scholarship without whose immense labors such an edition as this could never happen, among them William Jaggard, Samuel Tannenbaum, Walther Ebisch and Levin Schücking, Gordon Ross Smith, Charles Shattuck, Larry Champion, James Harner, Trevor Howard-Hill, and the countless compilers of the annual bibliographies in Shakespeare-Jahrbuch, PMLA, Shakespeare Bulletin, and Shakespeare Quarterly; and one must also mention here the invaluable concordances of Marvin Spevack and Trevor Howard-Hill.

It is a pleasure also to recognize several particular contributors. Peter Blayney kindly made available his edited text of Q1, and Frank Brownlow generously provided the computer discs of his text of Harsnett’s Declaration. John Nitti’s electronic wizardry made possible the computer-assisted analysis of textual variants and of the typesetting preferences of Folio compositors B and E, and Todd Bender prepared a useful concordance of the Variorum text. Robert K. Turner and John Murphy offered expert advice on textual study, Brian Vickers on Shakespearean vocabulary, Patrick Ford on Celtic myth, Edward Langhans, Judith Milhous, and Robert Hume on the Restoration stage, Ronald Harris on Geoffrey of Monmouth, and James Lattis on eclipses. The arduous and exacting work of textual collation of editions was done by student assistants—John C. Hill, Becky Bohan, Vivian Foss, and (for Q2) Elizabeth Reinwald; whatever errors may have escaped detection are my responsibility. Jane Behrend searched exhaustively through the OED to help elucidate Shakespeare’s possible meanings, and Leslie Eldridge, Pua Johnson, and William Rogers guaranteed the accuracy of quotations and citations. I owe a debt of gratitude to Judith Altreuter, Kathleen Fitzpatrick, James Hatch, David F. Cope, and other MLA staff, and to Julia Flanders and Kitto Weikert for tagging the edition.

This edition was also the happy beneficiary of much institutional support. I hope that its appearance helps to justify the trust shown long ago by the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation and the National Endowment for the Humanities, whose generous awards allowed work on the edition to begin in earnest. The Graduate School of the University of Wisconsin has likewise helped to maintain momentum by repeated grants for student project assistants; and research funds bestowed through the Dickson-Bascom Professorship in the Humanities have in a variety of ways helped ensure that this edition would reach fruition. It has been my good fortune to find myself in a University of Wisconsin Department rich in colleagues so distinguished as Shakespearean and Renaissance scholars, such as Helen White, Mark Eccles, Madelaine Doran, Ruth Wallerstein, Merritt Hughes, and many other luminaries and their superb students. Kevin Donovan wishes to thank the Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost of Middle Tennessee State University for a release from teaching duties in the Fall 2007 term, and to thank the Folger Shakespeare Library for a short-term fellowship in August 2007. Among the many research libraries on both sides of the Atlantic which made available their resources and the help of their staffs, special thanks must go to the incomparable Folger Library; to the Furness Memorial Library at the University of Pennsylvania and its former directors William Miller and Georgianna Ziegler; to the Library of Congress and the British Library; to the Bodleian and the Library of Trinity College, Cambridge; to the Boston Public Library and the New York Public Library, in particular for the latter’s Performing Arts division at Lincoln Center; to the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Garrick Club; and to the Shakespeare Centre Library at Stratford. I would need another scholarly lifetime adequately to thank the staff of the superb Memorial Library at the University of Wisconsin: its past Director, Lee G. Konrad, and the Director of Libraries, Kenneth B. Frazier, have afforded me many years of working space and have maintained a special collection of Shakespeare editions, commentaries, and scholarship that can scarcely be matched by any other university library in this country. These courtesies have been continued by the recently appointed Director, Edward Van Gemert, Vice Provost.
And finally—my late wife, Dr. Jane Boyle Knowles, whose love, loyalty, and unfaltering support have been a lifelong cause for wonder and gratitude.

div.head: Acknowledgements for the Digital Edition
div.p: The production of each NVS digital edition was conducted by a team of scholars and researchers and made possible by the Modern Language Association’s Executive Council that awarded the Center of Digital Humanities Research (CoDHR) at Texas A&M a grant to publish NVS editions online, making them freely available to scholars, educators, students, and performers via an open access, interactive web application. Each digital edition contains the complete text of each play along with a full collation of textual notes from the earliest editions to the present, including extensive previous commentary.

The physical Variorum volume includes a CD-ROM that contains an XML-encoded version of the contents, rendering the work as a PDF that is text-searchable with internal links for easy navigation. A special thanks to Julia Flanders, Professor of the Practice in English and the director of the Digital Scholarship Group in the Northeastern University Library, for XML-encoding the physical volume and for consulting with the NVS team at Texas A&M who used the XML-encoded text to publish this edition online at https://newvariorumshakespeare.org/.

This digital edition was published online on [date to be added], as part of a series of digital editions created for the NVS project. The project was officially launched at the World Shakespeare Congress (WSC) in Singapore in 2019 by the NVS team, which at that time included Laura Mandell (Principal Investigator and Director of the Center of Digital Humanities Research), Katayoun Torabi (Project Manager), Anne Burdick (NVS site designer and Chair of Media Design Practices at ArtCenter College of Design in Los Angeles), Bryan Tarpley (Lead Developer at CoDHR and NVS back-end developer), Will McLean (front-end developer and interaction designer), and Texas A&M graduate student researchers Kayley Hart and Lindsey Jones. Since its debut at the WSC, the NVS project has transitioned to Texas A&M University’s Department of English. There, the current NVS team—comprising Robert Stagg (Principal Investigator and NVS Director), Katayoun Torabi (Project Manager and Digital Editor), Kris May (Associate Digital Editor), and Dorothy Todd (Associate Digital Editor)—have worked in close collaboration with General Editors Paul Werstine and Eric Rasmussen, and under the guidance of the NVS Board chaired by Lena Cowen Orlin to bring this edition of King Lear online on [date to be added].

Special thanks are extended to the many faculty, staff, and student researchers who contributed to this volume, in addition to those mentioned above. We gratefully acknowledge the efforts of Inhoo Kim (Graduate Research Assistant); Jade Gooden, Grace Hoelescher, Shyam Prasad Nagulavancha, Mounika Balivada, Andrew Hoyt, and Fernando Gonzalez Torres (Research Assistants); and Scott Kleinman (Associate Technical Editor from CSU, Northridge). For more information about those who made the digital edition possible, please visit our Contributors page: https://newvariorumshakespeare.org/contributors/.

div.head: Plan of the Work
div.p: This edition of King Lear has four main parts: (1) a text of the play reprinted with little change from its first edition in the Quarto of 1608 (Q1), with additional lines from the Folio of 1623 (F1); (2) textual notes recording significant departures from the Q1 and added F1 lines in seventy-seven editions of the play ranging in date from 1619 to 2000; (3) commentary on the meaning or the artistry of the text drawn from previous editions, dictionaries, commentaries, and critical works; and (4), an appendix, comprising the second half of this edition, containing general discussions of the play’s text, date, sources, critical and theatrical interpretations, and music. This appendix is followed by a bibliography and an index.

The text presented here is a synthetic one, designed to serve the main purposes of a Variorum edition. The Variorum text is not primarily for reading; rather, it provides a point of reference for several hundred years of editing, elucidation, criticism, and performance. It must necessarily include both Q-only and F-only lines because all of those lines have been subject to commentary and theatrical use. Passages added from F are marked with asterisks (*) at their beginning and end as well as at the start of each added typographic line; Q passages omitted from F are enclosed in half-brackets (⸢ ⸣). The choice of the Quarto as the primary text reflects the general belief today that it not only is the earliest edition but also offers the earliest version of the play, one close to Shakespeare’s original drafts, and that the Folio represents a later version incorporating changes made for various theatrical and artistic purposes. For a historical survey of editing and commentary, the first version is the most convenient starting point. For the same reason, both Q and F lines presented here are in their original, uncorrected states, so that the commentary may proceed from the beginning towards later changes. The result is a Variorum text that preserves all of the hundreds of original textual difficulties that have occasioned centuries of discussion, so that the textual and commentary notes concerning those difficulties may refer directly to them in the text. Were they to be removed from a critically edited text, they would need to be reconstructed all over again in the notes; leaving them in the text most efficiently serves the purposes of a Variorum commentary.

The text is a modified diplomatic reprint derived from the Shakespeare Quarto Facsimile (1939) of Q1 and the Norton Facsimile (1968) of F1, and collated against the facsimile texts in Michael Warren’s The Complete King Lear 1608–1623 (1989). It has been compared with the records of press-corrections in W. W. Greg’s Variants (1940), Charlton Hinman’s Printing and Proof-Reading (1963), and Peter Blayney’s The Texts of King Lear and Their Origins in order to ensure that only uncorrected readings of Q and F are reproduced in the Variorum text; the corrected Q and F readings are recorded in the textual notes and the appendix (see , ). This reprint does not reproduce typographical features such as the long s, ligatures, display and swash letters, and ornaments. Abbreviations printed as logotypes, one letter above the other, are reproduced as two consecutive letters, the second one superscript. Minor typographical blemishes such as irregular spacing, printing space-types, and wrong-font, damaged, turned, transposed, misprinted or clearly erroneous or missing letters or punctuation marks have been corrected, in most cases silently. If, however, the anomaly is likely to have any bibliographical significance, its correction is recorded in the appendix (). Where an apparent error is not clearly typographical, or where the correction is not an obvious one, the text has been left unaltered and various emendations have been recorded in the textual notes. No substantive emendation or semi-substantive change of an accidental detail has been made in the text. A few turned-over or turned-under lines of verse have been printed continuously, and such alteration has been recorded in the appendix. Q1’s verse lineation, even when erroneous, has been preserved, as has that of the added F-only lines.

Through Line Numbers (TLNs) based on the Folio typographic line are printed by fives in the right margin. All Q prose has been relined as in F to enable the use of this universal F-based numbering system. Where the Q verse line, as a result of F’s different verse lineation, includes parts of two F lines, a vertical stroke within the Variorum line indicates the F division, and the marginal TLN is a hyphenated number indicating inclusively the F TLN numbers for both halves of the Variorum (Q) line (see, e.g., lines 76–84). If a Q-only phrase obviously completes or amplifies an existing F line, or supplants some part of it, it takes the number of that F line or part-line (as at lines 769 and 829–30). However, discrete Q-only verse or prose lines for which there can be no counterpart TLN numbers in F are assigned their own plus numbers beginning from the last previous F line. Thus Q’s four verse lines, lacking from F between its lines 1220 and 1221, are numbered 1220+1, 1220+2, etc., as are similarly its prose lines 427+1–+3. When as in the last example parts of an F line remain at the beginning and end of the intervening Q-only passage, their incompleteness is indicated by hyphens after and before the marginal TLN numbers—here, 427- and -427. When parts of an F line appear on two lines in Q, the same TLN number appears opposite both Q lines (see, e.g., 177, 510). TLN numbers of lines in Lr. are used for all notes and cross-references within the edition. Inclusive line numbers corresponding to those in the Riverside edition of 1974 and the Spevack concordances are supplied in arabic numerals in the headlines of each page to allow passages to be located according to act-scene-line numbers rather than TLNs. The Riverside act and scene division is indicated by boldface arabic numerals in the right margin at the beginning of each scene. The beginning of each Quarto page is marked in the right margin by signature numbers in square brackets, and the beginning of each Folio column is marked in the right margin by signature-and-column indicators in parentheses.

The textual notes are based on a collation of the following editions. Each of these editions has been fully collated against all of the Q and F lines in the text of this edition, except for oxf2, cam4, and oxf4, each of which has been collated only against its relevant Q or F control text. Each entry below is preceded by the siglum representing that edition in the textual notes and in the appendix of unadopted conjectures. When not mentioned, the place of publication is London. When commentary from these editions is quoted in the commentary notes and the appendix, it is given fuller citation by the editor’s name and the date of publication.

div.p: The textual notes record alterations in the meaning or meter of the Variorum text as they are found in the editions collated. Mere spelling variants are ignored, as are misprints unless an error creates an English word or has been taken for one. A conjectural emendation is included in a textual note if the reading has been adopted in one of the editions collated, and it is recorded in the form printed in that edition; others are occasionally discussed in the commentary notes or (in most cases) are included in the list of unadopted conjectures (), along with mere repetitions of earlier conjectures. Only a few manuscript emendations of special interest are recorded. Alterations of capitalization, punctuation, and italics are ignored unless the alteration creates a different meaning. If the subject of a textual note is variant punctuation only, a word in the lemma that is repeated unchanged in the variant is replaced in the note by a swung dash (&swdash;), and the absence of punctuation is indicated by an inferior caret (⁁).

Variant lining affecting meter—verse as prose, prose as verse, verse as different verse—is noted. The elision or expansion of syllables is recorded only if the alteration shifts the word’s accent or alters the number of feet in a verse line. When words that may be elided must be elided to make regular verse (e.g., in the to one-syllable i’th), it is assumed that the elision was intended and no note is provided. The expression one verse line indicates that part-lines of verse shared by speakers have been typographically arranged to indicate that taken together they constitute a pentameter. Since successive part-lines in a verse context were apparently expected to be metrically linked and thus spoken or read as pentameters when possible, the textual notes do not record the numerous instances when later editors since v1793 have indicated by typographic means that part-lines adding up to nine, ten, or eleven syllables form one verse line; rather, only unusual or disputed linkages of part-lines are recorded.

Stage directions added or altered in later editions appear only if the action implied in the Variorum text is affected in a major way. Added stage directions calling for action that is clearly implied by the text are not recorded, nor are those calling in different words for essentially the same action as the stage direction in the text. Relocation of a stage direction within a speech or passage is recorded only if the alteration might affect meaning. The abbreviation subst. indicates that although their language differs, the collated stage directions have substantially the same significance.

Textual notes generally consist of a lemma taken from the Variorum text, then one or more variants from that lemma, as recorded from the editions collated. Editions are identified by the sigla listed above and on the end-papers of this edition. If an edition is not included within a note, its text is presumed to agree with the lemma, i.e., with the Variorum text. The agreements and disagreements of editions on variant readings are indicated by the following symbols and conventions:

item.expan: (between sigla) all collated editions between and including the two specified
(after a siglum) and all succeeding collated editions
except the editions specified (within the parentheses), which agree with the Variorum text
and all other editions collated but not already accounted for in the note
word of the lemma unchanged (while punctuation varies)
stage directions substantially the same despite variant wording
detail of staging added to the lemma or the previous variant

div.p: The following, partially fictional note illustrates several conventions: 459 Fut] &swdash; Qq, ard1, nlsn, rid&sigrange;ban, folg2+; om. F1&sigrange;cap (−blair), knt, cam4; ’Sfoot oxf1; But Q3; Tut jen etc. The Variorum (Q1) text reads Fut and is followed by all the editions listed formulaically up to the first semi-colon; the next variant is the omission of the word from all the editions listed up to the next semicolon; then follow three substitutions for the lemma, the first two unique and the last adopted by jen and all other editions not otherwise identified. Fut is adopted by Q1 and Q2, ard1, nlsn, thirteen editions from rid to ban, and all editions (three of them) from folg2 onwards. The word is omitted by all editions from F1 through cap except for the fictional blair, which agrees with the original Fut; it is omitted also by cam4, and by the whole family of Knight editions collated (knt1, knt2, knt3). (A family siglum indicates only those editions collated: thus theo includes theo1, theo2, and theo4, but not theo3 and theo5.) Because Q3 was not fully collated, it is not included in the family siglum Qq; its unique reading But is included separately in the note only because of its special interest.

The following notes illustrate special kinds of variants: 620-1 lubbers,…againe⁁] &swdash; Q1(u); &swdash;⁁…&swdash;, Q1(c)+ Here only punctuation is at issue: the comma in the uncorrected state of Q1 is relocated in the corrected state; the caret indicates its place of absence in each variant, and the swung dashes (or lemma signs) stand for (and so avoid the repetition of) the invariant words. Only variant punctuation that makes a significant difference of meaning is recorded, and minor differences of rhetorical emphasis are ignored; thus the significant separation by a comma of againe from its following word tarry is recorded because it changes the syntactical relationship of the two words, but other possible punctuations in later editions—e.g., a dash or colon—which make a functionally equivalent syntactical separation would not be recorded. Similarly the comma (not shown) after tarry is significant because (according to contemporary usage) it divides one independent clause from the next; later substitutions of a rhetorically heavier stop—e.g., a semicolon, colon, dash, period, or exclamation mark—would be ignored unless they had some further significance than the division of the two clauses. 874 Kent] Ad. disguised as Caius evns&sigrange;ban, folg2+ (subst.) Here several editions add to the entrance direction the detail of Kent’s disguise, in various wordings that give substantially the same information. 1202 foole] foil warburton conj. apud han2, warb conj., han1 This note indicates that a reading adopted in han1 (1743) without acknowledgment of its source was later attributed to Warburton both in han2 (1745) and in warb (1747). Especially when conjectures first appear in a manuscript, there is often no way to ascertain that an editor later was aware of that source; the note simply records how early such an emendation was proposed, and gives the form in which it first later appeared in an edition.

The line-by-line commentary notes seek not only to elucidate the text but also to trace the history of the criticism to which a word or passage has been subjected, and to represent the whole range of opinion offered upon it, excluding only the patently erroneous, and occasionally adducing evidence to qualify the doubtful. The comments included in the notes are necessarily a selection; usually the earliest example of an interpretation is given unless a later one seems more clear, accurate, or explicit, and later repetitions of the same idea are ignored. All words and phrases which the OED describes as not in current standard use are defined, and all passages which have been annotated by a number of commentators are annotated here. All quotations are enclosed in quotation marks (to set them off from paraphrase or from the present editor’s comments) and are reproduced as in the source, except that titles of plays or books are regularized to italic, and comments wholly in italics are rendered in roman. Square brackets represent intervention by the editor(s) of this volume; square brackets within the original quotations are transformed to angle brackets (<>). The spelling and punctuation of the works cited are retained, except that if the beginning or end of a sentence has been omitted but a complete sentence remains, it is provided with a beginning capital and a final period. Omissions within quotations are indicated by ellipsis points, and paragraph breaks that fall within such omissions are not reproduced. Act-scene-line references to Lr. within the quotations have been replaced by TLN numbers within brackets; references to other plays are given both in TLN numbers and in Riverside act-scene-line numbers. Quotations of other Sh. plays are taken from the most authoritative Folio or Quarto text; specifically, the following plays are quoted from the superior quartos: Ado, 1H4, 2H4, Ham., LLL, MND, MV, Oth., Per., R2 (+ F1), Rom., Tit., TNK, and Tro. Biblical quotations are generally from the Geneva Bible (1560). Commentators are identified by last name only; the following parenthesis refers the reader either to the list of editions above—e.g., Foakes (ed. 1997)—or to the bibliography—e.g., Foakes (1993, p. 27). Whenever possible, roman numerals for act, scene, volume, etc. are given in arabic; a colon separates volume from page, and a period separates other entities—book, part, canto, stanza, etc.

In general the style of quotation and citation used in the commentary is also used in the appendix, save that the paragraphing of long quotations is preserved, and the beginning of each new page is indicated by an italic page number within brackets.
